stem: A vendor offers to sell equipment with deferred payment: Rs 3,000 at the end of each year for 4 years instead of a lump-sum payment today. The applicable discount rate is 8% per annum. What maximum lump-sum amount should a buyer agree to pay today to make the deferred deal equally attractive?  [Given: (1.08)^4 = 1.3605, (1.08)^(-4) = 0.7350]

per_option_rationale.rationale: Using the FV formula rather than PV gives 3000 x (1.3605-1)/0.08 = 3000 x 4.506 = Rs 13,519; this is the future value of the annuity, not the present value.
Summing the four undiscounted payments gives 3000 x 4 = Rs 12,000, ignoring the time value of money.
Multiplying the correct PV by (1.08) as if payments start at period zero (annuity-due) gives 9937.50 x 1.08 = Rs 10,733, incorrectly using the annuity-due adjustment for ordinary annuity payments.

explanation: The maximum fair lump-sum equals the present value of all future payments. PV = A x [1-(1+i)^(-n)]/i = 3000 x (1-0.7350)/0.08 = 3000 x 3.3125 = Rs 9,937.50.

explanation_sections.punchline: The PV of the annuity is the highest lump sum a rational buyer should pay - paying more would make the deferred scheme cheaper.
explanation_sections.lesson: PV of an ordinary annuity uses the discount factor [1-(1+i)^(-n)] not the growth factor [(1+i)^n - 1]; confusing them gives the future value instead.
explanation_sections.timing: 80 seconds. Direct annuity PV formula. Trap: option 1 uses FV formula; option 3 applies annuity-due adjustment.
